title: Women often opt for self-collection HPV screening, new studies show

analysis.time: Published on 2026-07-29. Event dates not specified in the evidence.
analysis.location_and_population: Singapore (study 1) and outpatient opioid treatment program patients in the United States (study 2). Study 1: 640 women aged 30-69. Study 2: 194 patients, with 174 eligible (89%), 19 recently screened, and 1 ineligible.
analysis.event: Two studies examined women's response to HPV self-sampling testing. Both studies found that when offered, women prefer self-collection over clinician testing. The Singapore study was published in the Annals of Family Medicine, and the U.S. study was published in JAMA Network Open.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Singapore study: 56.5% of women in the intervention group underwent HPV screening compared to 42.8% in the usual-care group. High-risk HPV detection was 3.1% in the intervention group versus 0.3% in the usual-care group. study: 158 (90.8%) of eligible patients agreed to self-collection testing; 30 tested positive for HPV (7 for HPV-16/18, 23 for other high-risk strains).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Singapore study: Offering self-sampling alongside clinician sampling significantly increased screening uptake and high-risk HPV detection. study: Self-collection testing was feasible and acceptable with high patient eligibility and uptake. Follow-up care was provided for 16 of the 30 patients with positive tests. The studies suggest self-collection could improve screening rates in underserved populations.

analysis.brief_en: Two recent studies highlight women's strong preference for self-collection HPV testing when offered. In Singapore, a study of 640 women found that providing self-sampling options increased screening uptake to 56.5% compared to 42.8% in the usual-care group, with a higher detection rate of high-risk HPV strains (3.1% vs. 0.3%). Similarly, a U.S. study involving 194 patients in an opioid treatment program found that 90.8% of eligible participants agreed to self-collection testing, with 30 testing positive for HPV. Both studies, published in the Annals of Family Medicine and JAMA Network Open respectively, conclude that self-collection testing is feasible, acceptable, and effective at expanding screening rates in underserved populations, potentially reducing healthcare disparities and cervical cancer mortality.

title: Self-Sampling Boosts HPV Detection and Increases Cervical Cancer Screening Rates - Bioengineer.org

analysis.time: Publication date: July 27, 2026. Event period: Not explicitly stated, but the trial was conducted in Singapore with results reported in 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Target population: Women aged 30 to 69 due for cervical cancer screening. Study sample: 650 women randomly assigned to intervention (325) or usual care (325) arms.
analysis.event: A pragmatic randomized controlled trial in Singapore tested whether offering self-collected HPV samples alongside clinician-collected specimens would improve cervical cancer screening participation and HPV detection rates. The intervention group was offered clinician sampling first, with self-sampling if declined, while the usual-care group received clinician sampling only.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: HPV detection rates: 3.1% in intervention arm vs. 0.3% in usual-care arm. Screening uptake: 56.6% in intervention arm vs. 42.8% in usual-care arm. Seven of ten high-risk HPV cases were among previously unscreened women, with five detected via self-sampling. No explicit risk level stated, but improved detection suggests reduced risk of missed cervical cancer opportunities.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The trial supports patient-centered screening strategies with self-sampling as an accessible alternative. Equity concerns noted: women with lower education were less likely to choose self-sampling. The study is a completed randomized controlled trial with clear results, but limitations include potential generalizability beyond Singapore and the need for equity-sensitive design improvements.

analysis.brief_en: A pragmatic randomized controlled trial in Singapore demonstrated that offering self-collected HPV samples alongside clinician-collected specimens significantly improved cervical cancer screening rates and HPV detection. Among 650 women aged 30-69, the intervention group achieved 56.6% screening uptake (vs. 42.8% in usual care) and 3.1% HPV detection (vs. 0.3%). Notably, seven of ten high-risk HPV cases were in previously unscreened women, with five detected via self-sampling. This suggests self-sampling lowers barriers without compromising high-risk HPV identification, though equity concerns persist for women with lower education. The findings support patient-centered strategies to improve both first-time and ongoing screening participation.
analysis.summary_en: A pragmatic randomized controlled trial in Singapore demonstrated that offering self-collected HPV samples alongside clinician-collected specimens significantly improved cervical cancer screening rates and HPV detection. Among 650 women aged 30-69, the intervention group achieved 56.6% screening uptake (vs. 42.8% in usual care) and 3.1% HPV detection (vs. 0.3%). Notably, seven of ten high-risk HPV cases were in previously unscreened women, with five detected via self-sampling. This suggests self-sampling lowers barriers without compromising high-risk HPV identification, though equity concerns persist for women with lower education. The findings support patient-centered strategies to improve both first-time and ongoing screening participation.

title: Cervical Cancer From HPV : A Preventable Disease - โรงพยาบาลรามคําแหง

analysis.time: Published on July 27, 2026; event context not specified in evidence.
analysis.location_and_population: Thailand; women aged 35–60, particularly affected by cervical cancer.
analysis.event: Confirmed: Cervical cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer among women in Thailand, with over 6,000 new cases and approximately 2,600 fatalities reported annually. The disease is preventable through early detection via medical screenings.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Over 6,000 new cases annually; approximately 2,600 fatalities. HPV is present in 99.7% of cervical cancer cases. High-risk HPV strains can cause abnormal cell changes leading to cancer over time.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Advanced HPV DNA testing (90% sensitivity) is available at Ramkhamhaeng Hospital's Obstetrics and Gynecology Clinic using PCR. Early detection through screening (Pap smear combined with HPV testing) can prevent progression. Sample collection occurs during pelvic exams, with results in seven days. Last updated: August 25, 2021.

analysis.brief_en: Cervical cancer is the most common cancer among women in Thailand, with over 6,000 new cases and 2,600 deaths annually. Human Papillomavirus (HPV) is the primary cause, detected in 99.7% of cases. While conventional Pap smears have limitations, advanced HPV DNA testing offers high sensitivity (90%) for early detection. Ramkhamhaeng Hospital provides PCR-based HPV testing, combining sample collection during pelvic exams with results within seven days. Early intervention through regular screening can prevent progression, as precancerous lesions take years to develop. Women aged 30+ are advised to undergo combined Pap smear and HPV testing every three years if normal, or more frequently if inconclusive. Prevention remains key, with early detection being the most effective strategy.
analysis.summary_en: Cervical cancer is the most common cancer among women in Thailand, with over 6,000 new cases and 2,600 deaths annually. Human Papillomavirus (HPV) is the primary cause, detected in 99.7% of cases. While conventional Pap smears have limitations, advanced HPV DNA testing offers high sensitivity (90%) for early detection. Ramkhamhaeng Hospital provides PCR-based HPV testing, combining sample collection during pelvic exams with results within seven days. Early intervention through regular screening can prevent progression, as precancerous lesions take years to develop. Women aged 30+ are advised to undergo combined Pap smear and HPV testing every three years if normal, or more frequently if inconclusive. Prevention remains key, with early detection being the most effective strategy.

title: Delhi HC Lets HPV Vaccine Drive Continue Amid Safety Plea

analysis.time: Published on July 31, 2026; event occurred on July 29, 2026, with the vaccination campaign launched on February 28, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: India, nationwide campaign targeting adolescent girls aged 14, with approximately 1.2 crore girls identified as eligible across 36 states and Union Territories.
analysis.event: The Delhi High Court declined to grant an interim stay on India’s HPV vaccination campaign, allowing it to continue while questions about informed consent, safety evidence, and monitoring remain under examination.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Over 55 lakh doses administered in India; approximately 120 recipients reported minor events such as headache or nausea; no immediate harm demonstrated to justify suspension; campaign targets cervical cancer prevention.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Court directed the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Indian Council of Medical Research, and Central Drugs Standard Control Organization to file detailed replies; vaccination continues while legal challenge is pending; safety and consent procedures remain under examination.

analysis.brief_en: The Delhi High Court has allowed India’s HPV vaccination campaign to proceed after declining an interim stay, citing no immediate harm to justify suspension. The court, however, emphasized the need for further examination of informed consent, safety evidence, and monitoring protocols. The nationwide campaign, targeting adolescent girls aged 14, has already administered over 55 lakh doses, with approximately 120 minor adverse events reported. The petitioners, including a gynecologist and health entrepreneur, raised concerns about bodily autonomy, informed consent, and potential pressure on health workers. The government defended the vaccine’s global safety record, citing use in 160 countries. The court has sought detailed responses from health authorities while the vaccination drive continues.

The court, however, emphasized the need for further examination of informed consent, safety evidence, and monitoring protocols. The petitioners, including a gynecologist and health entrepreneur, raised concerns about bodily autonomy, informed consent, and potential pressure on health workers. title: Seegene Advances Comprehensive HPV and STI PCR Testing with Large-Scale Clinical Evidence - BioPharma APAC

analysis.time: Publication date: 28 July 2026. Event date: 29 July 2026 (announcement date). Analysis period: 42 months (test data collection).
analysis.location_and_population: Global healthcare institutions (through the Global Million Clinical Study). Affected population: Individuals undergoing HPV and STI testing, with focus on reproductive tract infections and cervical cancer risk assessment.
analysis.event: Seegene announced a comprehensive syndromic PCR-based testing approach for reproductive tract infections (RTIs), detecting both STIs and HPV simultaneously. This follows the launch of the Global Million Clinical Study on 8 July 2026. The announcement is based on analysis of 60,000 test results and is presented as scientific evidence supporting a new global standard for PCR testing.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Analysis of 60,000 test results showed STI pathogens were detected in 82% of HPV-positive cases, HPV in 46% of STI-positive cases, and co-detection in 71% of positive cases. The findings support the potential application of concurrent STI testing with HPV screening for identifying asymptomatic STIs, assessing co-infections, and supporting reproductive health evaluations. No explicit risk level is stated.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Seegene is validating the clinical utility of comprehensive HPV & STI testing through the Global Million Clinical Study, using STAgoraTM for real-world data accumulation and statistical evaluation. The initiative aims to establish scientific evidence for new global PCR testing standards. The analysis is based on internal company data and represents preliminary findings that require further validation through the ongoing study.

analysis.brief_en: Seegene has announced a comprehensive syndromic PCR-based testing approach for reproductive tract infections that simultaneously detects sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and human papillomavirus (HPV). Based on analysis of 60,000 test results collected over 42 months, the company found that STI pathogens were present in 82% of HPV-positive cases, HPV in 46% of STI-positive cases, and co-detection in 71% of positive cases. These findings support the potential value of comprehensive testing for cervical cancer risk assessment and reproductive health diagnostics. The announcement follows Seegene's launch of the Global Million Clinical Study on July 8, 2026, which aims to generate scientific evidence for a new global standard of PCR testing by accumulating real-world clinical data from healthcare institutions worldwide.
analysis.summary_en: Seegene has announced a comprehensive syndromic PCR-based testing approach for reproductive tract infections that simultaneously detects sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and human papillomavirus (HPV). Based on analysis of 60,000 test results collected over 42 months, the company found that STI pathogens were present in 82% of HPV-positive cases, HPV in 46% of STI-positive cases, and co-detection in 71% of positive cases. These findings support the potential value of comprehensive testing for cervical cancer risk assessment and reproductive health diagnostics. The announcement follows Seegene's launch of the Global Million Clinical Study on July 8, 2026, which aims to generate scientific evidence for a new global standard of PCR testing by accumulating real-world clinical data from healthcare institutions worldwide.

title: HPV vaccination: Protecting girls today from cervical cancer tomorrow - standardmedia.co.ke

analysis.time: Published on 2026-07-26; Event context refers to ongoing HPV vaccination efforts in Kenya since 2019, with a policy change to single-dose vaccination in November 2025.
analysis.location_and_population: Kenya; Focus on girls aged 9-14 as the primary target group for HPV vaccination, with emphasis on reaching communities facing barriers to healthcare access.
analysis.event: Health opinion piece advocating for HPV vaccination as a preventive measure against cervical cancer, highlighting Kenya's national immunization program and its shift to a single-dose schedule in 2025.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Kenya reports approximately 5,845 new cervical cancer cases and 3,591 deaths annually (GLOBOCAN 2022 data); Globally, 660,000 women were diagnosed with cervical cancer in 2022, with 350,000 deaths. The burden is heaviest in low- and middle-income countries.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Kenya introduced HPV vaccination in 2019, initially targeting 10-year-old girls, and transitioned to a single-dose schedule in November 2025 per WHO recommendations. Screening remains a complementary strategy for women aged 25-49, with HPV testing recommended for those over 30 where available. No current outbreak or investigation status is reported.

analysis.brief_en: Kenya faces a significant burden of cervical cancer, with approximately 5,845 new cases and 3,591 deaths annually. To address this, the country has implemented HPV vaccination as a key preventive measure, targeting girls aged 9-14 before potential exposure to the virus. In November 2025, Kenya transitioned from a two-dose to a single-dose HPV vaccination schedule, aligning with WHO recommendations to improve accessibility and reduce barriers in communities. While vaccination is crucial, it is not a replacement for cervical cancer screening, which remains essential for early detection in women aged 25-49. This integrated approach aims to reduce cervical cancer incidence and mortality by combining vaccination with regular screening and early treatment of precancerous lesions.

This integrated approach aims to reduce cervical cancer incidence and mortality by combining vaccination with regular screening and early treatment of precancerous lesions.

title: New Cervical Cancer Pill Could Stop HPV Before It Turns Cancerous

analysis.time: Publication date: July 27, 2026. Event date: Not explicitly reported, but the article discusses ongoing research and future availability.
analysis.location_and_population: Global focus with emphasis on India, where cervical cancer is the second most common cancer among women. Affected population: Women with persistent HPV infections, particularly those with high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN).
analysis.event: Development of an experimental oral therapy called SHetA2, which targets HPV proteins to prevent progression to cervical cancer. The therapy is not yet approved and is in clinical trials. Reported by: Ashima Sharda Mahindra for Times Now.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: In India, cervical cancer caused over 79,000 new cases and more than 36,000 deaths in 2024. Persistent high-risk HPV infection is responsible for nearly 85% of cervical cancer cases. SHetA2 aims to treat existing infections rather than prevent them. Risk level: Not explicitly stated.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The therapy is in early clinical trials, with larger human trials expected to take up to five years before regulatory approval. It is not intended to replace HPV vaccination or screening but to complement them. The final price has not been announced, but it is expected to be affordable as an oral small-molecule medicine. Source limitation: The article is a full original report body.

analysis.brief_en: A new oral therapy, SHetA2, shows promise in stopping persistent HPV infections from progressing to cervical cancer by targeting cancer-causing proteins. Developed by the University of Oklahoma and ICMR-NICPR, the therapy disrupts the interaction between the HPV-E7 protein and human cells, allowing the body's natural defenses to destroy the virus. While it cannot prevent HPV infection, it may benefit women with precancerous lesions or early-stage cervical cancer. In India, where cervical cancer is the second most common cancer among women, causing over 79,000 new cases and 36,000 deaths in 2024, this treatment could fill a critical gap. Larger clinical trials are underway, with potential availability in up to five years. The therapy is expected to be affordable and administered orally, reducing the need for hospital visits. Doctors emphasize that it will complement, not replace, HPV vaccination and screening programs.

title: New cervical cancer pill shows promise by stopping HPV from turning cancerous: How it works?

analysis.time: Published on July 29, 2026; event development ongoing with Phase 1 clinical trials completed, Phase 2 and 3 pending.
analysis.location_and_population: India; women with chronic HPV infections and abnormal cervical cells, particularly in areas with limited specialized treatment access.
analysis.event: Development of SHetA2, an oral anti-HPV drug candidate licensed by ICMR to Emcure Pharmaceuticals, aimed at preventing HPV-induced cervical cancer by targeting cancer-inducing proteins rather than the virus itself.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Cervical cancer ranks second among cancers in Indian women, with 79,000 cases and 36,000 deaths estimated in 2024; SHetA2 may provide additional defense but is not yet a substitute for existing prevention measures.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Phase 1 clinical trials show promising early results; Phase 2 and 3 trials pending to establish long-term safety and effectiveness; not yet approved for routine use; emphasizes continued reliance on vaccination and screening.

analysis.brief_en: India is advancing in cervical cancer prevention with SHetA2, an oral drug that targets HPV-induced cancer-causing proteins rather than the virus itself. Licensed by ICMR to Emcure Pharmaceuticals, SHetA2 aims to stop chronic HPV infections from progressing to cervical cancer. While Phase 1 trials show promise, further testing is needed before approval. Cervical cancer remains a major health threat in India, with 79,000 cases and 36,000 deaths in 2024. Experts stress that vaccination and regular screening remain critical until SHetA2 is fully validated.

title: Only 34 of 200 girls took HPV vaccine at Delhi camp: Debunking myths about safety, side effects and fertility

analysis.time: Published on July 29, 2026; event occurred during a recent free HPV vaccination drive in Delhi.
analysis.location_and_population: Delhi, India; approximately 200 eligible girls participated in the vaccination camp.
analysis.event: A free HPV vaccination drive in Delhi faced vaccine hesitancy, with only 34 out of 200 girls vaccinated due to parental concerns about safety, side effects, and fertility.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 34 out of 200 girls vaccinated; low uptake attributed to misinformation about HPV vaccine safety and potential effects on fertility; no reported cases of adverse effects or infections from the vaccine.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Healthcare providers are addressing misinformation through awareness campaigns; WHO and CDC endorse HPV vaccine safety; more vernacular communication between healthcare providers and families is needed to increase vaccine uptake.

analysis.brief_en: In Delhi, a free HPV vaccination drive saw only 34 out of 200 eligible girls receive the vaccine, primarily due to parental concerns about safety, side effects, and fertility. Despite evidence from the WHO and CDC confirming the vaccine's safety over 15 years of monitoring, misinformation persists. Experts emphasize that HPV vaccines prevent up to 90% of cervical cancer cases and are safe, with minor side effects like pain or swelling at the injection site. The low uptake highlights the need for better communication between healthcare providers and families to combat myths and build trust in vaccination efforts.
